vignette: Clara Varga stood at the corner of the alley, her gloves damp with rain, when the dispatch confirmed the subject was armed. She remembered the shout first, then the sudden shift in the air as three officers moved in. The moment coordination broke, an officer grabbed her forearm to pull her back from the scene, his grip tight and unannounced. The world narrowed to the smell of wet concrete, the sharp crack of a baton, and the overwhelming pressure of bodies colliding. What frightened her most was how completely the scene overtook her perception, how every sound and movement registered as immediate. When she later tried to reconstruct the night for the station captain, she lost the thread halfway through. She knew the sequence never lined up-whether the radio crackled before the first strike or after, whether her own feet had moved before or after the shout-left her grasping at smoke. She simply could not finish the account. For months after, the past did not stay where it belonged. When she closed her eyes on the ambulance bay floor, she felt the exact pressure on her bicep, the same metallic taste in her mouth. She had come to believe that the event was not a memory but a repeating condition. She began choosing her chair in the firehouse with deliberate precision, always tucking herself near the wall, back to the door, legs angled toward the exit. Her eyes tracked the hallway before stepping into the bay, constantly scanning for the sharp creases of tactical gear, the heavy cadence of boots, anything that carried the imprint of the officers who had harmed the man on the ground. Anything that reminded her of him made her step sideways, taking the long route through the parking lot. When a colleague reached out to tap her shoulder during a debrief, her breath caught, every muscle locking before she could force herself to turn. The habits settled over time. On calls, she positioned herself at the rear of the ambulance, gripping the rail, eyes sweeping the street for anything that resembled the alley. She stopped sitting in the front passenger seat during shifts, claiming it made her motion-sick, though the reality was her need for protected sightlines. When the burn in her chest rose, she noticed it only to shut it down. She never allowed herself to feel or express anger. The nausea followed in the quiet hours, a heavy pull in her stomach that she simply accepted as part of the shift. Her ex-husband had asked her once why she never stayed over, why she kept her keys in her pocket instead of leaving them on the counter. She could not explain the sudden panic of unfamiliar locks or the way her mind would jump to the worst possible sequence of events, so she stopped trying. The silence between them grew, then broke, and the divorce papers arrived before the first anniversary. Now, at thirty-one, Clara sat in a clinic chair waiting for her intake. She had chosen the seat closest to the exit, her knees drawn slightly inward. Her stomach turned again, familiar and unyielding, as the receptionist called her name. She was certain that if she kept moving, kept scanning, kept herself perfectly still, she could keep the past at bay. But the nausea had not stopped, and neither had the way her shoulders tensed at the slightest shift behind her. She had scheduled this appointment not because she knew how to fix the fractured pieces of her mind, but because she was exhausted from apologizing for existing in a body that no longer felt like her own. She hoped, somehow, for a way to lay the weight down without breaking. She was afraid that if she ever stopped watching the doors, she would never breathe easy again.
